content: The decision was made not to downgrade the evidence, as the differences observed between studies could be attributed to variations in perspectives. Skaathun et al. (1) and Pines et al. (2) evaluated the cost-effectiveness of HIV testing strategies from the perspective of healthcare providers, whereas Zulliger et al. (3) adopted a societal perspective. Additionally, Skaathun et al. (1) and Zulliger et al. (3) conducted their studies in the United States, while Pines et al. (2) carried out their research in Mexico. Regarding inconsistency, no downgrading was applied because the differences between studies were explainable by variations in healthcare systems. For example, Zhou et al. (4) and Sha et al. (5) conducted their studies in China, while Shahmanesh et al. (6) performed their research in South Africa. In terms of indirectness, Shahmanesh et al. (6) did not confirm whether the distributed HIV self-testing (HIVST) kits were actually used. Instead, they reported the cost per HIVST kit distributed. Furthermore, the comparators used in the three studies varied. For the cost per person tested, comparing social network approaches (SNA) with HIVST versus SNA with testing referral cards, the evidence was rated as high certainty. The cost per person tested ranged from $120 to $940. For the cost per person tested when comparing SNA versus peer distribution, the evidence was rated as moderate certainty, with costs ranging from $36 to $56. When evaluating the cost per person diagnosed, the evidence was rated as low certainty due to serious concerns about imprecision and indirectness. For example, the cost per person diagnosed when comparing SNA with financial incentives versus SNA without financial incentives ranged from $46 to $930, with moderate certainty. Similarly, when comparing SNA with financial incentives and peer referral versus SNA without financial incentives, the cost per person diagnosed ranged from $56 to $930, with moderate certainty. Inconsistency was not assessed in cases where only a single study was available. Imprecision was downgraded in instances where the event rate was less than 400. Indirectness was also downgraded in some cases due to differences in comparators or the lack of verification of HIVST kit usage. The references cited include studies by Skaathun et al. (1), Pines et al. (2), Zulliger et al. (3), Zhou et al. (4), Sha et al. (5), and Shahmanesh et al. (6), which provide detailed evaluations of the cost-effectiveness and implementation of various HIV testing strategies across different settings and populations.
